slides.title: For almost 100 years, we've quoted one finding about unfinished tasks.

slides.kicker: It began with a restaurant bill.
slides.body:
In 1920s Berlin, psychologist Kurt Lewin noticed something odd about waiters.

They could recall the details of a bill until it was paid. Then the details were gone.

slides.kicker: His student put it to the test.
slides.body:
Bluma Zeigarnik gave people a series of tasks and interrupted some of them.

In 1927 she reported that unfinished tasks were remembered far better than finished ones. The Zeigarnik effect was born.

slides.kicker: Her classmate asked a different question.
slides.body:
Maria Ovsiankina, also taught by Lewin, didn't ask what people remember. She asked what they do.

In her 1928 study, people interrupted mid-task tended to go back to it, often unprompted.

slides.kicker: The famous result proved hard to repeat.
slides.body:
Later experiments, in other countries, often found no real gap in memory between finished and unfinished tasks.

Still, the idea kept spreading.

slides.kicker: In 2025, someone added it all up.
slides.body: A review of 59 publications found no overall memory advantage for unfinished tasks.

Across the studies, about two in three interrupted tasks were picked up again.

Zeigarnik's effect may appear in some situations. It just isn't a general rule. Ovsiankina's tendency is.

slides.lead: The idea everyone repeats isn't always the one that survives the test.

slides.line: Save this for the next time you hear "studies show".

caption:
Unfinished tasks stick in your memory. That's the famous Zeigarnik effect, and a 2025 review of the research found it isn't a general rule.

What did hold up came from her classmate, Maria Ovsiankina: we tend to go back to what we left unfinished. 🔁

Which "fact" did you believe for years before finding out it was wrong?
